Benjamin Franklin had a peculiar fondness for swimming and retained his boyish skill in it to old age, even inventing swimming devices such as oval pallets for his hands and sandals for his feet to improve his swimming.
He complained that he never could acquire the virtue of order in his business, having a place for everything and everything in its place, and this failing followed him to the end of his life.

Benjamin Franklin died calmly and cheerfully, surrounded by his grandchildren and friends, and a few days before his death he expressed that he hoped not to live many years longer, showing acceptance and peace at the end of his life.
He left behind a mass of writings, "full of his own kindness, humor, and wisdom, to perpetuate his influence, and sweeten the life of coming generations."
Franklin was honored and remembered by various societies, public celebrations, and monuments, including illuminations, fireworks, and the erection of an obelisk in Boston to commemorate his memory.

The Congress of the United States and the National Assembly of France paid distinguished honors to his memory, with Congress resolving to wear mourning and Mirabeau in France declaring, "Franklin is dead! The genius, that freed America and poured a flood of light over Europe, has returned to the bosom of the Divinity."
